parts.move: state the magnetic flux definition and the angle convention in the formula
parts.prompt: State the formula for the magnetic flux through a surface, defining each symbol and stating precisely what the angle θ measures.
scheme: Φ = BA cos θ
B is the flux density, A the area of the surface
θ is the angle between the field direction and the NORMAL to the surface (not the plane)
parts.answer: Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ, where B is the flux density, A the area, and θ the angle between the field and the surface's normal. A field in the plane of the loop (θ = 90°) threads zero flux — a detail that decides whether an emf can ever be induced.

parts.move: explain what must change, and in what way, for an emf to be induced
parts.prompt: State Faraday's law in words, and explain which three experimental changes can each produce an induced emf in a stationary coil.
scheme: Faraday: induced emf equals the (negative) rate of change of flux linkage, ε = −d(NΦ)/dt
The field B can grow or shrink (electromagnet current changing)
The area of the loop can change (a coil expanding or contracting)
The orientation can change (rotating the loop alters cos θ)
parts.answer: Faraday's law: the induced emf is minus the rate of change of flux linkage, ε = −d(NΦ)/dt. Since Φ = BA cos θ, a stationary loop can still see change through three doors: B varying (an electromagnet ramping), A varying (the loop deforming), or θ varying (the loop rotating — the geometry of every generator).

parts.move: derive the necessity of Lenz's opposition from energy conservation
parts.prompt: Suppose the induced current aided the change in flux instead of opposing it. Explain the runaway outcome, and why this proves the minus sign in Faraday's law.
scheme: Aiding current would increase the flux change, which would increase the induced emf further
The emf would grow without limit — energy appearing from nowhere
The opposition (Lenz) means the inducing agency must do positive work, which is exactly the electrical energy delivered
parts.answer: If the induced current reinforced the flux change, the change would accelerate itself: more flux change, more emf, more current, more change — an energy-creating runaway. The minus sign forbids it: by opposing the change, the induced effect forces the external agent to do work, and that work is precisely the electrical energy extracted. Lenz's law is energy conservation written into circuit theory.

parts.move: compute the flux through a coil at a stated rotation angle
parts.prompt: A circular coil of radius 5.0 cm with its plane initially perpendicular to a 0.20 T field rotates 60° about a diameter. Calculate the flux before and after the rotation.
scheme: Initially the normal is parallel to B: Φ₀ = BA = 0.20×7.85×10⁻³ = 1.57 mWb
After 60°: Φ = BA cos60° = 0.785 mWb
The flux halves at 60° because cos60° = 0.5
parts.answer: The coil's area is 7.85×10⁻³ m². With its normal along the field, Φ₀ = 1.57 mWb; rotating 60° multiplies by cos60° = 0.5, giving 0.79 mWb. The continuous version of this swing is the sinusoid every generator delivers.

parts.move: compute the motional emf of a rod cutting field lines
parts.prompt: A 0.30 m conducting rod slides at 4.0 m s⁻¹ along rails in a 0.50 T field perpendicular to the rod's motion. Calculate the emf induced between the rod's ends, and state which end is positive if the field is into the page and the rod moves right.
scheme: Flux swept per second = B × area rate = BLv
Right-hand rule: field into page, motion right → force on positive charges upward, top end positive
parts.answer: The rod sweeps out flux at rate BLv, inducing ε = 0.50×0.30×4.0 = 0.60 V. With the field into the page and motion to the right, positive charges feel an upward magnetic force: the top of the rod is positive. Fleming's right-hand rule gives the same verdict in one gesture.

parts.move: reject field strength as the criterion for induction
parts.prompt: Two set-ups: (i) a coil resting in a huge steady 5.0 T field; (ii) a coil in a tiny 0.010 T field that doubles in 0.10 s. A student claims set-up (i) must induce more emf because its field is 500 times stronger. Calculate the relevant quantity for each and correct the claim.
scheme: Set-up (i): steady field → dΦ/dt = 0 → no emf at all
Set-up (ii): ε ∝ dΦ/dt = A×0.010/0.10 = 0.10A per second — nonzero
A 5 T static field induces nothing; a 0.01 T changing field induces something
The emf depends on rate of change, not magnitude
parts.answer: The 5.0 T field induces exactly zero emf — flux that never changes drives nothing. The 0.010 T field doubling in 0.10 s gives dΦ/dt = 0.10A Wb s⁻¹ and a genuine emf. Induction rewards change, not strength: a 500-times-weaker field that changes beats an unchanging giant.

parts.move: compute the emf while a coil is withdrawn from a field at constant speed
parts.prompt: A 250-turn rectangular coil of area 4.0×10⁻³ m² sits entirely inside a 0.15 T field. It is pulled completely out in 0.20 s. Calculate the mean induced emf, and the total charge that flows if the circuit's resistance is 5.0 Ω.
scheme: Flux change per turn: ΔΦ = BA = 0.15×4.0×10⁻³ = 6.0×10⁻⁴ Wb
Flux linkage change: NΔΦ = 250×6.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.15 Wb-turns
Charge: Q = εt/R = 0.75×0.20/5.0 = 0.030 C (or Q = NΔΦ/R)
parts.answer: Removing the coil changes its flux linkage by NΔΦ = 250×0.15×4.0×10⁻³ = 0.15 Wb-turns in 0.20 s, a mean emf of 0.75 V. The charge driven round the 5.0 Ω loop is Q = NΔΦ/R = 0.15/5.0 = 0.030 C — independent of how fast you pull, a favourite exam subtlety.

parts.move: transfer induction reasoning to eddy-current braking and its speed dependence
parts.prompt: A magnetic train brake pushes a strong magnet toward a spinning aluminium wheel and the wheel slows without contact. Explain the mechanism and why the braking force vanishes as the wheel slows to rest.
scheme: The changing flux through the metal induces circulating eddy currents
By Lenz's law those currents produce fields opposing the relative motion — a drag force
As speed falls, dΦ/dt falls, so the induced currents and the braking force shrink toward zero at rest
parts.answer: The moving wheel cuts flux, inducing eddy currents in the aluminium; by Lenz's law their fields oppose the motion, producing drag. But the induced currents scale with the rate of flux change, so the braking fades with speed and vanishes at rest — a contactless brake that is gentle at the end of the stop, exactly where friction brakes are harshest.

parts.move: transfer flux-change reasoning to an induction hob and why it heats only the pan
parts.prompt: An induction hob's coil carries alternating current, yet the glass surface stays cool while an iron pan heats rapidly. Explain the physics of the selectivity.
scheme: The AC coil produces an alternating flux through the pan's base
The pan, being a conductor, carries induced (eddy) currents that dissipate energy as heat (helped by iron's resistance and hysteresis)
The glass is an insulator: no induced currents, no heating — the energy appears only in the metal
parts.answer: The hob's alternating current threads a changing flux through whatever sits above it. In the iron pan that flux drives eddy currents, and the pan's electrical resistance converts them to heat (with hysteresis adding its share). The glass top conducts no current, so induction skips it entirely: the pan becomes the heating element, and the surface merely holds it.

parts.move: combine the rotating-flux geometry with the induced emf's sinusoidal time dependence
parts.prompt: A 200-turn coil of area 1.2×10⁻² m² rotates at 50 rev s⁻¹ in a 0.080 T field. Calculate the peak emf and the r.m.s. emf, and state the output frequency.
scheme: ω = 2π×50 = 314 rad s⁻¹
ε_rms = ε₀/√2 = 42.6 V at 50 Hz
parts.answer: Rotating at 50 rev s⁻¹ (ω = 314 rad s⁻¹), the peak emf is NABω = 200×1.2×10⁻²×0.080×314 = 60 V, with an r.m.s. value of 43 V at 50 Hz. The formula chains the flux geometry to the sinusoid's slope in one step — a generator is Faraday's law with a crank handle.

parts.move: combine gravity-induced speed change with the flux profile to predict a measured pulse
parts.prompt: A bar magnet is dropped through a stationary coil connected to a datalogger. Sketch the emf-time trace in words and explain the sign change and the asymmetry between the two peaks.
scheme: As the magnet approaches, flux through the coil grows: an emf of one sign
As it recedes, flux falls: an emf of the opposite sign — the trace crosses zero at maximum flux
The magnet accelerates through, so the second peak is narrower and taller (faster flux change)
The areas of the two peaks are equal: each corresponds to the same total flux swing
parts.answer: The trace shows one peak of each sign. Entering, the flux grows — an emf of one polarity; at the coil's centre the flux momentarily peaks and the emf crosses zero; leaving, the flux collapses and the emf reverses. Because the magnet accelerates as it falls, the exit happens faster: the second peak is taller and briefer. But the two peaks enclose equal areas — the same flux swung each way, just at different rates. A datalogger can read g off a magnet's fall.
